disclaimer: Original study guide keyed to public curriculum; course content itself lives at the source.

checkpoints: Define idempotency in one sentence and explain why `terraform apply` is idempotent but `aws s3 mb` is not.
List three concrete ways drift can appear in a team-managed AWS account.
Task: given a plan that shows `~ update in-place` on three resources and `-/+ destroy and recreate` on one, identify which change carries the highest risk.
keyConcepts: Declarative vs imperative configuration
Desired state, actual state, and the diff (delta) between them
Idempotency: applying the same definition twice produces no further changes
Configuration drift and drift detection
Convergence loop: plan, apply, reconcile
Mutable vs immutable infrastructure patterns
IaC benefits: versioning, peer review, repeatable environments
labs: Write a shell script that creates an S3-style local directory structure imperatively, then rewrite it declaratively as a Terraform local_file set and compare rerun behavior.
Introduce an out-of-band change to a managed resource (e.g., rename a file), then run `terraform plan` to observe drift detection output.
Create two environments with identical intent but different tooling (one with shell scripts, one with Terraform); document which one survives a partial-failure rerun.
Simulate a click-ops change and a code change to the same resource, then practice resolving them by making code the source of truth.
objectives: Contrast declarative desired-state definitions with imperative step-by-step scripts in terms of idempotency and failure recovery.
Explain configuration drift: how it forms, why it matters, and how a reconciling engine detects it.
Describe the core loop of modern IaC: declare desired state, compute a diff, converge reality.
Identify which problems IaC solves (repeatability, auditability, review) and which it creates (state management, blast radius).
modules.title: The IaC Mental Model: Declarative State vs. Imperative Steps

checkpoints: Write from memory: a variable block with type `list(string)`, a default, and a validation rule.
Explain when `locals` are preferable to `variable` defaults.
Task: given a resource that needs a value known only after another resource is created, show the correct reference syntax.
keyConcepts: Block types: terraform, provider, resource, variable, output, data, locals, module
Resource addressing and implicit/explicit dependency graph (`depends_on`)
Variable types, defaults, validation blocks, and sensitive flags
Data sources as read-only queries against provider APIs
Expressions: `for`, ternary, `merge`, `lookup`, splat `[*]`, dynamic blocks
Built-in functions for string, collection, and encoding operations
File layout conventions: main.tf, variables.tf, outputs.tf, versions.tf
labs: Build a `null_resource`-free local lab with the `local` and `random` providers: generate a random pet name, write it to a file, expose it as an output.
Add a validated variable (e.g., allowed regions list) and intentionally pass an invalid value to observe the validation error.
Use a data source (e.g., `data.local_file` or provider-specific availability zones) and interpolate its attributes into a resource.
Refactor repeated blocks into a `dynamic` block driven by a map variable.
objectives: Author `resource` blocks with correct addressing (`type.name`) and attribute references.
Distinguish input variables, local values, outputs, and data sources by purpose and data flow.
Write HCL expressions: conditionals, for-expressions, splat operators, and type conversions.
Structure a configuration directory: provider blocks, version files, and root vs child module layout.
modules.title: HCL: Resources, Variables, Outputs, Data Sources, Expressions

checkpoints: Name three things stored in the state file that are NOT in your .tf files.
Explain why committing terraform.tfstate to git is an anti-pattern.
Task: plan shows a resource will be recreated after a teammate renamed it in code — which state command avoids the recreation?
keyConcepts: State file as the mapping of resource addresses to provider-side object IDs
State locking (e.g., DynamoDB, native backend locks) and why concurrent writes corrupt state
Remote backends: S3/GCS/Azure with versioning and encryption
State versioning, backups (`terraform.tfstate.backup`), and manual inspection
`terraform import` addressing and the follow-up of writing matching configuration
State surgery commands: `mv`, `rm`, `pull`, `push`, `replace-provider`
Workspaces as named state partitions within one backend
labs: Initialize with a local backend, apply, then migrate the state to a remote backend (S3 + DynamoDB lock or Terraform Cloud free tier) using `init -migrate-state`.
Create a resource manually (out-of-band), then `terraform import` it into state and write matching configuration until `plan` is empty.
Simulate a stale lock: kill a run mid-apply in a scratch backend and practice `force-unlock` with the lock ID.
Refactor a resource rename using `terraform state mv` and verify plan shows zero changes.
objectives: Explain what the state file records (bindings between configuration and real objects) and why Terraform cannot function without it.
Configure a remote backend with state locking to make team workflows safe.
Execute `terraform import` to bring pre-existing infrastructure under management, and `terraform state mv` to refactor without recreation.
Recover from common state failures: lock held by a crashed run, and state/backend mismatch.
modules.title: State: The File, Locking, Remote Backends, and Import

checkpoints: Write the constraint that allows patch updates within 5.31.x but nothing newer.
Explain the difference between the lock file and the version constraint.
Task: a Registry module's new minor version changes a default — where do you pin to prevent surprise?
keyConcepts: Provider as a plugin bridging Terraform core to an API surface
`required_providers` and `required_version` constraint syntax
Public vs private module registries; module source addresses
Module interface design: variables.tf contract, outputs.tf, README with examples
Version pinning strategy for production: exact pins, lock file, upgrade cadence
Provider schema changes and why upgrades can alter plans
`terraform init` dependency resolution and the plugin cache
labs: Consume a public Registry module (e.g., a VPC or S3 module) pinned to an exact version; then deliberately loosen the pin and observe what `init -upgrade` changes.
Author a module that provisions a standardized logging bucket (naming convention, encryption, lifecycle); publish it to a local path source and then a git source.
Add `terraform-docs` output to your module README and enforce it in a pre-commit hook.
Practice a provider major-version upgrade in a scratch workspace: read the changelog, adjust configuration, review the plan diff.
objectives: Declare provider requirements with version constraints and explain semantic-versioning implications of `~>` vs `>=`.
Consume a Registry module and pin it to an exact version.
Author a reusable child module with a clean interface: typed inputs, documented outputs, minimal side effects.
Manage the dependency lock file (`.terraform.lock.hcl`) and provider installation in CI.
modules.title: Providers and Modules: Registry, Version Constraints, Authoring

checkpoints: Rank these by precedence: environment variable TF_VAR_x, -var flag, terraform.tfvars, x.auto.tfvars.
Give one concrete risk of using workspaces for prod/staging separation.
Task: design the backend key layout for three environments and two regions.
keyConcepts: Workspaces as alternate state files sharing one configuration and backend key prefix
Directory-per-environment as the stronger isolation boundary (separate state, separate credentials)
tfvars layering: `terraform.tfvars`, `*.auto.tfvars`, `-var-file` precedence order
Environment promotion: same module version, environment-scoped inputs
Backend key naming schemes per environment
When workspaces are acceptable (ephemeral feature environments) vs when they are not
labs: Stand up dev and prod as separate directories sharing one child module, with per-environment tfvars; apply dev, then promote the module version to prod.
Demonstrate precedence: set a value in `terraform.tfvars`, override it in `prod.auto.tfvars`, override again with `-var`, and record the winning value at each step.
Create two CLI workspaces against one backend and show how a resource name collision appears (or is avoided) in the plan.
Document a promotion runbook: the exact command sequence to move a change from staging to prod.
objectives: Compare the two environment-isolation models: Terraform workspaces vs separate directories/backends.
Layer variable values with `.tfvars` files (common, environment-specific, secrets) and CLI `-var` overrides.
Design an environment promotion path: dev → staging → prod with identical modules and differing inputs.
Explain why workspaces are a poor fit for strong production isolation.
modules.title: Workspaces and Environments: Isolation Strategies and tfvars Layering

checkpoints: Why must CI apply the saved plan file instead of running plan again at apply time?
Name two situations where `-target` is justified and one where it masks a real problem.
Task: plan shows an unexpected `-/+` on a stateful resource — list your investigation steps before approving.
keyConcepts: `terraform plan -out` artifact as the reviewed unit of change
Plan output notation: `+`, `~`, `-`, `-/+` and what triggers replacement
`-target` / `-replace` semantics and the partial-state risk they introduce
`lifecycle` meta-arguments: `prevent_destroy`, `create_before_destroy`, `ignore_changes`
Refresh-only plans and their role in drift review
`terraform destroy` vs removing configuration then applying
Applying the saved plan file (not re-planning) in automation
labs: Generate a plan to a file, inspect every proposed change, apply the saved file, then re-run plan to confirm empty.
Taint one resource with `-replace`, apply, and document the replacement sequence and any downtime observed.
Mark a database-class resource `prevent_destroy`, attempt to remove it from configuration, and handle the resulting error deliberately.
Produce a destroy plan for a scratch environment and walk the teardown order before applying it.
objectives: Run a disciplined plan/apply cycle: plan artifact saved, reviewed, then applied with the same file.
Use `-target` and `-replace` surgically and explain why routine targeting is an anti-pattern.
Apply destroy hygiene: staged teardown order, `-destroy` plans, and protecting critical resources with `prevent_destroy`.
Diagnose plan output: additions, changes, destroys, replacements, and data-source reads.
modules.title: Planning Workflows: plan/apply Discipline, Targeted Changes, Destroy Hygiene

checkpoints: Contrast `terraform apply` from a laptop with Argo CD auto-sync: who is the actor converging state in each?
Explain what 'prune' does and one scenario where it is dangerous.
Task: a PR plan shows a security-group opening 0.0.0.0/0 — where in the workflow should this be caught?
keyConcepts: Git as the single source of truth; declarative manifests and drift reconciliation
Argo CD Application CRD: source repo/path, destination cluster/namespace
Sync status vs health status; out-of-sync detection and diff view
Auto-sync, prune, self-heal: power and blast-radius tradeoffs
Sync waves and hooks for ordered rollouts (CRDs before workloads)
PR-driven infra: atlantis-style plan comments, CODEOWNERS, protected branches
Secret strategies: Sealed Secrets, External Secrets Operator, SOPS-encrypted values
labs: Install Argo CD in a local kind/k3s cluster, register a git repo with a sample app, and practice manual sync after an out-of-band `kubectl` edit.
Enable auto-sync with prune on a scratch app, make a git commit, and watch the reconciliation; then trigger a bad commit and practice rollback via git revert.
Build a PR workflow on a Terraform repo: CI runs `fmt`, `validate`, and posts `plan` output as a PR comment; merge is blocked until approved.
Store an encrypted secret with SOPS or Sealed Secrets in git and have the cluster decrypt it at sync time.
objectives: Describe the GitOps contract: desired state lives in git; an agent reconciles the cluster toward it.
Operate Argo CD primitives: Application, sync, refresh, auto-sync vs manual sync, and sync waves/hooks.
Design a pull-request workflow for infrastructure: plan-on-PR, required approvals, apply-on-merge.
Manage secrets in GitOps without committing plaintext (sealed/encrypted references and external secret operators).
modules.title: GitOps Flow: Git as Source of Truth, Argo CD Sync, PR Workflows for Infra

checkpoints: Does `sensitive = true` encrypt the value in the state file? Explain the real protection it provides.
Write one OPA/Conftest-style rule in pseudocode that blocks public S3 buckets.
Task: list the ordered gates a production apply pipeline should enforce from commit to apply.
keyConcepts: Plan review checklist: replacements, permission changes, data exfiltration surface
Policy-as-code engines: Sentinel/OPA/Conftest evaluating plan JSON
Common guardrails: mandatory tags, encryption-at-rest, region allowlists, no `0.0.0.0/0` ingress
`sensitive = true` markings and why state still contains the values
Secrets injection: vault providers, environment-backed credentials, short-lived tokens
State encryption at rest and access control on the backend
Blast radius: module granularity, environment staging, canary applies
labs: Export `terraform plan -out` to JSON and write a Conftest/OPA rule that fails the build on unencrypted storage or missing tags.
Mark an API key variable `sensitive`, apply, then inspect the state file to prove the value is still present — then move the secret to a vault data source.
Add a CI gate: `terraform fmt -check`, `terraform validate`, and your policy check must all pass before apply is permitted.
Run a tabletop incident: a bad apply deleted a queue — write the rollback procedure using state history and git revert.
objectives: Build a layered review process: human plan review, automated lint/validate, and policy gates before apply.
Express infrastructure guardrails as policy-as-code (allowed regions, required tags, no public buckets).
Handle secrets correctly: never in state-visible plaintext, rotation strategy, least-privilege provider credentials.
Design a blast-radius reduction strategy: small modules, staged rollouts, and rollback plans.
modules.title: Testing and Safety: Plan Review, Policy-as-Code, Secrets Handling
